title: Settling, Blurring, Fitting, Flicking & Recycling
description: A mosaic that relaxes itself, a blur that ramps, a fallback font that never jumps, a switch you can flick, and a million rows in forty nodes.

drops.title: Cells That Settle
drops.description: Lloyd's algorithm turns a random scatter of Voronoi cells into an even, organic honeycomb — and animates itself doing it.
drops.concept: Random points make terrible Voronoi cells: slivers beside giants. Lloyd relaxation iterates one move — replace each point with the centroid of its own cell, then rebuild the diagram — and the mosaic settles into near-uniform tiles. Three stages here: a live relaxation with a falling drift readout, a frozen-vs-converged comparison from one seed, and a version that keeps relaxing around a pointer field. The Voronoi is built by half-plane clipping against a nearest-neighbour shortlist, so the whole drop stays dependency-free.

interaction.mouse: Drag across the third mosaic to push a repulsion field through the cells as they relax.
interaction.click: Re-seed from the panel, and tune cell count, step size and cell gap.
interaction.touch: The pointer field is pointer-event driven, so dragging works the same on touch.

drops.title: Blur With a Gradient
drops.description: Masking a blurred pane fades its opacity, not its radius — stacking thin panes ramps the blur itself.
drops.concept: The common progressive-blur snippet puts one backdrop-filtered pane behind a gradient mask, which fades how much of the blur you see while the radius stays constant — a blanket with an edge. Real progressive blur stacks thin panes whose radii fall off geometrically, each masked to its own overlapping slice so the seams never align. The drop shows the single-pane version beside the stack, a scroll container dissolving into both its edges, and the same stack rotated onto the inline axis.
drops.source: Jonothan Hunt — “Progressive blur on the web”

interaction.mouse: Scroll the panels to move content under the veils and compare the two edges.
interaction.click: Set layer count, peak radius and band height; drop layers to 1 to see the blanket.
interaction.touch: Each panel scrolls independently; the rail scrolls horizontally.

drops.title: Fallbacks That Don't Jump
drops.description: size-adjust and the *-override descriptors reshape a fallback font so the webfont swap moves nothing.
drops.concept: A fallback almost never shares metrics with the face it stands in for, so the swap shifts every line beneath it — the last big layout shift most sites still ship. The @font-face descriptors size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override let you reshape the fallback to occupy the target's box before the swap happens. Two panels swap the same face side by side with a live px-shift readout, an overlay shows the baselines converging, and a solver derives the numbers from Canvas text metrics. Every face is a local() lookup, so the page needs no network.
drops.source: MDN Web Docs — @font-face/size-adjust and the metric-override fallback technique

interaction.mouse: Compare the two marker lines while the swap runs.
interaction.click: Swap the font by hand, or let the solver measure both faces and fill the descriptors in.
interaction.touch: All controls are buttons and sliders; the comparison stacks on narrow screens.

drops.title: A Switch You Can Flick
drops.description: Click, drag or flick — a fast gesture commits on velocity even from below the halfway line.
drops.concept: Most web switches are a checkbox with a transition, which only answers the click. Adding a pointer track lets a drag follow the finger exactly, and tracking velocity lets a flick commit on direction rather than distance, the way the native control does. The thumb stretches in proportion to its speed, so hard gestures deform and slow ones do not. It stays a real role=switch button, so Space, Enter and the arrow keys never touch the drag code, and a live trace plots position against velocity.
drops.source: Adam Argyle / web.dev — “Building a switch component”

interaction.mouse: Click to toggle, drag the thumb to scrub, or flick and release below halfway.
interaction.click: Tune spring stiffness, thumb stretch and the commit point from the panel.
interaction.touch: Pointer capture makes drag and flick behave identically under a finger.

drops.title: A Million Rows, Forty Nodes
drops.description: One tall spacer keeps the scrollbar honest while a fixed pool of row elements is recycled as you scroll.
drops.concept: A list only has to exist where it can be seen. A spacer sized rows × rowHeight gives the scrollbar a truthful range, the visible slice is translated into place, and a pool of elements just big enough for the viewport plus overscan is reused rather than rebuilt — which is what separates smooth virtualisation from the stuttering kind, since the cost is allocation and style recalc, not scrolling. A live counter shows the node count staying flat at a million rows, with chat-reverse and sticky-header table variants.

interaction.mouse: Scroll or fling any of the three lists; watch the live element count hold steady.
interaction.click: Type a row number to jump straight to it; change row count, height and overscan.
interaction.touch: Momentum scrolling is handled by the browser; the scroller only reacts to scroll events.
